brief: What two years of working alone actually taught me

slots.standfirst: It is, eventually. The first eighteen months are something else, and nobody describes that part honestly because it does not sound like an achievement.
slots.item1: Why the good days stopped being the point
slots.item2: The lesson that took a year longer than it should have
slots.coverNote: None of this was obvious at the time

slots.para1: For most of the first year I believed the problem was that I did not have enough time. I had all of it. What I did not have was anything forcing a decision, and without that I could rewrite the same page for a week and call it work.
slots.para2: What changed was arbitrary: I started telling people dates. Not because the dates were meaningful, but because a promise made out loud is a constraint you cannot quietly renegotiate at two in the afternoon.
slots.pullLine: Speed was never about effort. It was about having fewer places left to hide.

slots.para1: I spent a long time looking for better ideas, on the assumption that the work was mostly a search problem. It is not. Nearly everything I have made that worked was the fourth or fifth attempt at something I had already tried and abandoned.
slots.para2: The uncomfortable version of this is that the ideas were never the bottleneck. I simply had not done any of them enough times to be good at them, and finding a new one felt more like progress than repeating an old one.
slots.pullLine: I kept chasing better ideas. What I needed was a better loop.

slots.para1: This is the part that sounds like freedom and functions like a hazard. There is no review, no colleague noticing you have been stuck for three weeks, and no natural moment where somebody asks what you are actually working on.
slots.para2: I ended up manufacturing the check: one person, once a week, who I had to tell what I had finished. Not a mentor and not accountability theatre — just somebody who would notice the same answer twice.
slots.pullLine: Autonomy is not the absence of pressure. It is having to build your own.

slots.para1: For a year I described what I did in a way that was accurate and useless. People were polite about it and then hired somebody whose sentence they could repeat to a colleague without getting it wrong.
slots.para2: When the sentence got shorter, the work got easier to sell, and none of the underlying skill had changed in the meantime. That still annoys me, and it is still true.
slots.pullLine: People pay when they can explain to somebody else why they did.

slots.para1: The weeks where nothing shipped used to read as evidence that the whole arrangement was a mistake. They were mostly just weeks. Averaged over a quarter they disappear entirely, but a bad week is experienced at full volume and a quarter is not experienced at all.
slots.para2: The only thing that helped was writing down what happened each week, badly, in one line. Not for the record — for the version of me who would otherwise remember the whole month as a failure.
slots.pullLine: You judge a year by its worst week unless you write the others down.

slots.para1: Almost everything above was available to me in advance. People had written it down; I had read it and decided it applied to somebody with different circumstances, which is what everybody does with advice that would require changing something.
slots.para2: So I have no clean lesson to offer about this part. Reading it does not do very much, and I do not think it did much for me either until the same mistake had cost me something I could count.
slots.pullLine: Advice is cheap because taking it is the expensive part.

slots.eyebrow: If you are somewhere in the first year
slots.standfirst: Not a plan, not a system, not a rebuild of how you work. One date, said out loud to somebody who will remember it.
slots.closingLine: Everything else on this list took me two years. That one takes an afternoon.
slots.signoff: It works because you cannot renegotiate with them
